United States. The proposed legislation affects only transactions taking place under the jurisdiction of the United States. Therefore, transactions may go on in other parts of the world without regard to the proposed legislation. However, the United States is one of the more important nations in the trade in wildlife and wildlife products, and the proposed legislation will have far-reaching effects on world trade, not only on direct U.S. transactions but as an example to other nations. A feature of the proposed legislation that would broaden the impact of trade restrictions is the expansion of the endangered species list to include those species "likely within the foreseeable future to become threatened with extinction."

Thereby, more species and subspecies would be subject to trade controls.
The trade impact has a positive side in the possibility that successful restoration of species may ultimately return the endangered population to the point where it can again be cropped on a long time basis. By careful management, populations of one-time commercial importance may again be utilized for their trade value.
Group 2 species will frequently become subject to management programs before their populations have declined to non-exploitable levels and will thus be able to support long term sustained-yeild cropping. It is reasonable to argue that this is an economically wiser course of action than unrestrained exploitation and will result in greater economic yields over time. The proposed legislation then, by permitting preventative action, will result in an economic saving through encouraging wise management before a species is reduced to near-extinction. The costs of expensive recovery programs for severely depleted species will also be avoided in many instances.
